articles.title_original: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.12798v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Post-training a language model can induce surprising behavioral changes far beyond the intended training target. We study two particularly striking examples: emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning on a narrow dataset leads to misaligned behavior in unrelated contexts, and subliminal learning (SL), where a student model inherits a teacher's misalignment through seemingly benign training data. We examine how the training data, evaluation data, and training method shape where and how strongly misalignment transfers between data and models. We characterize the data by the domain of a prompt (its topical context) and its task (the function the model performs), and we build natural-language and synthetic datasets organized as domain-task grids. We find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts that share the task of the fine-tuning data than to prompts that share its domain. In the synthetic setting, tasks that the model has learned well spread misalignment more broadly. For SL, we go beyond SFT (supervised fine-tuning) to off-policy distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution and, to our knowledge for the first time, on-policy distillation, where the teacher only scores tokens sampled by the student. Misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under SFT and at a level comparable to off-policy distillation. Unlike SFT, where the teacher both generates the data and supervises the student, distillation lets us separate the two. With the teacher fixed, the data change how much misalignment the student inherits, but the teacher determines to which domains and tasks it transfers most strongly. Together, these results show how data and training influence the extent and patterns of emergent and subliminal misalignment.

articles.title_original: Known By Their Actions: Fingerprinting LLM Browser Agents via UI Traces
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.14786v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As LLM-based agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, a natural question arises: can websites passively identify which underlying model powers an agent? Doing so would represent a significant security risk, enabling targeted attacks tailored to known model vulnerabilities. Across 14 frontier LLMs and four web environments spanning information retrieval and shopping tasks, we show that an agent's actions and interaction timings, captured via a passive JavaScript tracker, are sufficient to identify the underlying model with up to 96\% F1 within a fixed harness. Although fingerprints are harness-specific, with cross-harness transfer falling to near chance, pooling traces across harnesses recovers model identification at 0.74 to 0.81 Macro-F1. We further show that strong classifiers can be trained from roughly one third of the available traces, and that identification improves steadily as more events are observed. Injecting randomised timing delays between actions substantially degrades classifier performance, but does not provide robust protection: a classifier retrained on delayed traces largely recovers performance. We release our code and a labelled corpus of agent traces at https://github.com/KabakaWilliam/known_actions.

articles.title_original: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.16245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into the online platforms where humans exchange opinions; large language models (LLMs) have been polishing users' posts on LinkedIn and providing context for content shared on X. While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We address this gap via a combination of empirical and theoretical analyses. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. Building on this observation, we introduce a mathematical model of opinion dynamics in which an AI system sits between users on a social network, transforming the opinions they express and perceive. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.

articles.title_original: Automated Root-Cause Subclassification and No-Code Fix Generation for Invalid Bug Reports
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.17561v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Issues faced when using software are reported in the form of bug reports. However, many bug reports are invalid, meaning they do not require code changes, and are resolved with a no-code fix. Manually determining the root cause of the invalid bug reports and providing actionable resolutions by the customer support causes a serious waste of resources. Our goal is to introduce a standardized taxonomy for root-cause oriented invalid bug report subclassification, and perform experiments to test the accuracy of various approaches on invalid subclassification and no-code fix generation. We study how different configurations perform on a gold-standard benchmark we have created. Using a manually curated benchmark for higher quality analysis, we experimented with vanilla LLMs, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and agentic web search to identify invalid subclasses and generate no-code fixes. We evaluated the results against manually labeled ground truth data that includes the invalid subclass and no-code fixes from the original bug reports. We measured subclass detection performance with weighted F1-Score, and assessed no-code fix suggestions using BERTScore and Judge LLM success rates. For subclassification, retrieval augmented generation achieves the highest overall performance with 0.66 weighted F1, slightly outperforming vanilla LLMs at 0.65 and agentic web search at 0.64. At the subclass level, performance peaks at 0.85 F1 for Non-reproducibility and 0.79 for Feature Request and Question, while Wrong Version remains the most challenging with scores between 0.00 and 0.29. For no-code fix generation, agentic web search achieves the highest overall Judge LLM success rate at 68.9%, compared to 64.4% for RAG applications and 64.9% for vanilla LLMs, with subclass-level peaks of 87.4% for Working as Designed and 72.2% for Question.

articles.title_original: DOTRAG: Retrieval-Time Reasoning Along Paths
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.18760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) faces significant challenges in complex relational retrieval tasks, particularly in densely connected knowledge graphs where the number of possible paths grows rapidly with reasoning depth. Existing GraphRAG retrieval algorithms either rely on rigid, predefined heuristics to identify relevant graph context or employ costly LLM-based reasoning to guide graph traversal. To address these limitations, we propose DotRAG, a lightweight, training-free GraphRAG retrieval algorithm that uses large language model (LLM) reasoning to narrow the search space and recover task-relevant relational paths. During indexing, DotRAG constructs an entity-relation knowledge graph, generates a graph-wide overview summarizing its contents, and leverages graph reachability indexing to avoid expensive online graph traversals. At query time, the LLM uses this overview to identify promising graph regions and hypothesizes relationship sequences connecting graph information to the query. The LLM then performs targeted relational searches, using graph constraints to restrict the candidate pool progressively. On MetaQA 2-hop queries, DotRAG achieves 97.78% retrieval recall and 51.27% F1, compared to the best baseline scores of 34.74% and 6.33%, respectively. On STaRK-MAG, DotRAG achieves 85.07% recall on 2-hop queries while demonstrating greater computational efficiency than reasoning-based GraphRAG baselines, with 12.2x lower retrieval latency than HopRAG.

articles.title_original: Variance Reduction for Gradients from Diffusion Teachers
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.21489v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Pretrained diffusion models serve as frozen teachers for pipelines such as text-to-3D, single-step distillation, and data attribution. The teacher gradients these pipelines consume are expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise, estimated by Monte Carlo (MC). Each MC draw requires expensive upstream work (rendering, simulation, encoding), so estimator variance dominates compute cost. We introduce CARV, a compute-aware variance-accounting framework that casts these gradients as a classical two-stage sampling problem with asymmetric per-level costs. This motivates a hierarchical MC estimator that amortizes each expensive upstream computation by reusing it across cheap diffusion draws, with within-unit variance further reduced by timestep importance sampling (IS) and stratified inverse-CDF sampling. CARV delivers 2 to 3x effective compute multipliers on text-to-3D and data attribution without changing the objective. In text-to-3D, reuse provides most of the gain and IS with stratification adds about 25%. In single-step distillation, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude but do not improve downstream FID, marking the regime where MC variance is no longer the bottleneck.

articles.title_original: AnyMo: Geometry-Aware Setup-Agnostic Modeling of Human Motion in the Wild
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.22715v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As wearable and mobile devices become increasingly embedded in daily life, they offer a practical way to continuously sense human motion in the wild. But inertial signals are highly dependent on the sensing setup, including body location, mounting position, sensor orientation, device hardware, and sampling protocol. This setup dependence makes it difficult to learn motion representations that transfer across devices and datasets, and limits the broader use of wearable IMUs beyond closed-set recognition. We introduce AnyMo, a geometry-aware framework for setup-agnostic human motion modeling. AnyMo uses physics-grounded IMU simulation over dense body-surface placements to generate diverse and plausible synthetic signals, pre-trains a graph encoder from paired synthetic placement views and masked partial observations, tokenizes multi-position IMU into full-body motion tokens, and aligns these tokens with an LLM for motion-language understanding. We evaluate AnyMo on three complementary tasks: zero-shot activity recognition across 14 unseen downstream datasets, cross-modal retrieval, and wearable IMU motion captioning, where it improves average Accuracy/F1/R@2 by 11.7\%/11.6\%/22.6\% on HAR, increases zero-shot IMU-to-text and text-to-IMU retrieval MRR by 15.9\% and 28.6\%, respectively, and improves zero-shot captioning BERT-F1 by 7.5\%. These results support AnyMo as a generalist model for wearable motion understanding in the wild. Project page: https://anymo-project.github.io.

articles.title_original: Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward: Towards Principled One-step Generator RL
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.24001v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent advances in one-step text-to-image generation have enabled real-time synthesis with remarkable efficiency and quality. Previous reinforcement learning methods for one-step generators combine image-space reward optimization with diffusion noisy-space distribution matching. This paradigm brings challenges due to a mismatch between terminal reward optimization and the underlying generative dynamics. As a result, optimization tends to exploit stochastic degrees of freedom, often improving reward at the expense of image fidelity. To address this issue, we propose Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a data-free trajectory-level alignment framework derived from Integral KL minimization. DIDR propagates the RLHF-optimal reward-tilted clean-image distribution across all noise levels along the diffusion trajectory. We show that this objective admits the same minimizer as clean-image RLHF, while naturally inducing the Diffused Reward Score (DRS), which acts as a reward-driven correction to the reference score function. To make this practical, we further introduce the Diffused Reward Proxy (DRP), an efficient estimator of DRS based on differentiable short-step denoising. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIDR consistently Pareto-dominates existing one-step SDXL baselines. Moreover, when transferred to a 6B DiT backbone (Z-Image), DIDR surpasses its 50-step teacher in preference alignment while requiring only a single generation step. Code: https://github.com/Junyi-W/DIDR

articles.title_original: StakeBench: Evaluating Language Understanding Grounded in Market Commitment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.26074v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Existing financial NLP benchmarks often rely on labels supplied by outside observers, measuring how language is perceived rather than what speakers have committed to in the market. We introduce StakeBench, an evaluation framework for language understanding grounded in market commitment. StakeBench links 560,876 comments from 2,261 resolved markets to verified position, action, and market-odds records across Polymarket and Manifold. Supervision is derived from observable market behavior. Position sides, post-comment trading actions, and market-odds trajectories replace human annotation. Four diagnostic tasks test whether models detect market commitment, identify the revealed side, anticipate future action, and perform collective odds projection. Three commitment-aware metrics measure alignment with revealed preferences rather than perceived sentiment. Validity audits and explicit interpretation boundaries help distinguish observable commitment signals from latent belief and causal market-odds impact. Across 15 LLMs and 18 topics and platform settings, models partially recover position-side signals, with Directed Accuracy from 0.506 to 0.599, but show structural failures on later tasks. Ten of the fifteen models collapse to one or two action labels in future action anticipation, and no model consistently improves on the naive odds-direction baseline in collective odds projection. Model scale is not correlated with performance, finance-domain tuning does not improve revealed-side identification, and platform incentives strongly shape higher-order results. StakeBench is packaged with evaluation code and dataset under CC-BY 4.0.

articles.title_original: Unified Panoramic Geometry Estimation via Multi-View Foundation Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.26368v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Geometry estimation from perspective images has greatly advanced, maturing to the point where off-the-shelf foundation models are able to reconstruct 3D scene structure not only from multi-view imagery, but even from a single view. A natural extension is 3D reconstruction from panoramas, with the exciting prospect of recovering a full 360-degree scene from a single panoramic image. In this work, we introduce PaGeR (Panoramic Geometry Reconstruction), a framework to lift powerful 3D foundation models designed for perspective imagery to the panorama domain. Our strategy is to start from a pre-trained transformer for 3D reconstruction and turn it into a unified high-performance model that predicts scale-invariant depth, metric depth, surface normals, and sky masks from both perspective and omnidirectional images, in a single forward pass. By keeping architectural changes to a minimum and mixing perspective and panoramic images during training, PaGeR retains the rich 3D prior of the underlying foundation model while learning to also estimate geometrically consistent 360-degree scenes from single panoramas. We extensively test our method in both indoor and outdoor environments and find that it delivers state-of-the-art performance and excellent zero-shot performance across a wide range of scenes. Code, data and models are available $\href{https://github.com/prs-eth/PaGeR}{\text{here}}$.

articles.title_original: Unified Synthesis of Compositional Speech and Sound from Free-Form Text Prompts
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.28063v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generating unified audio that naturally integrates speech and sounds from free-form text prompts remains challenging. For example, the prompt ``A fast drum roll ends with a cymbal crash, after which a man shouts: `Come on!'.'' describes several events that should appear in order and form a coherent recording rather than independent tracks that lack coherent temporal and semantic interactions. Current methods broadly follow two paradigms: pipeline methods couple separate text-to-sound and text-to-speech models, while unified models rely on a single generator that still requires structured, multi-field prompt inputs. Both paradigms require upstream prompt decomposition or rewriting, limiting free-form flexibility and risking cascading errors. To enable direct generation from free-form prompts within a single model, we introduce PlanAudio, an end-to-end framework that maps unconstrained free-form text to unified audio without intermediate prompt preprocessing. To address the challenges of direct free-form generation, PlanAudio integrates latent planning into a single autoregressive framework, predicting continuous audio layout before acoustic token synthesis. We construct a large-scale training corpus and introduce Free-Form Unified Audio Generation Benchmark (FUAG) for evaluation, both spanning speech, sound, and joint speech-and-sound generation. Experiments show that a single PlanAudio outperforms existing pipeline and unified baselines on speech-and-sound generation, while remaining competitive with specialist models on speech and sound generation. Further analysis validates the effectiveness of audio layout planning over textual planning, acoustic planning, and direct generation. Sample Available: https://planaudio.github.io/PlanAudio2026/.

articles.title_original: Pruning and Distilling Mixture-of-Experts into Dense Language Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2605.28207v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is now the dominant architecture for frontier language models, yet it requires all expert parameters to be loaded in memory, making it less preferable for memory-constrained deployment. Existing compression methods reduce the number of experts but the output remains an MoE model with the same fundamental limitation. We present the first systematic framework for converting a trained MoE into a standard fully dense architecture: experts are scored, selected, and grouped, then concatenated into a dense FFN and refined by knowledge distillation from the MoE teacher. We evaluate 7 scoring, 5 grouping, and 2 magnitude scaling methods across a range of selected expert counts on Qwen3-30B-A3B, yielding 350 configurations. We find that the choice of scoring method is the most impactful, with our novel diversity-aware scoring consistently outperforming prior methods on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and GPT-OSS-20B. Under a controlled comparison at matched parameter count, MoE-to-dense outperforms dense-to-dense pruning by +6.3 pp in average downstream accuracy after ~4B-token distillation at 1.6x faster training wall-clock speed.

articles.agent: AI担当エージェント
articles.title_original: With Tools or Because of Tools? Tracing Capability Gains in Multimodal Agents
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.02357v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tool-augmented multimodal agents show strong benchmark gains, often taken as evidence that agents have learned to use tools. We argue that this interpretation can be premature: a tool-call trace alone does not show whether the tool supplied answer-critical information. We study two representative ``thinking with images'' agents, Thyme and DeepEyesV2, across real-world understanding, OCR, chart understanding, and mathematical reasoning. Each agent is compared with its Tool-Free counterpart and with a Pure-Text Reasoner trained from the same source pool without tool-calling trajectories. Tool access yields little consistent aggregate improvement, does not reliably reduce generated-token cost, and leaves only a small tool-only solved set: 93% of DeepEyesV2's tool-solved problems and 96% of Thyme's are also solved by at least one non-tool setting. Mechanism ablations further show that the full tool-use loop does not consistently outperform either the tool-call format or the returned execution result alone. In the settings we study, the analyzed agents appear to learn tool-calling patterns more reliably than tool-contributed capabilities, suggesting that evaluation should distinguish tool availability from whether tools actually expand what agents can solve.

articles.agent: AI担当エージェント
articles.title_original: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.07537v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Surveys of hallucination classify errors by how an output relates to its source, and often explain them by the model's structure: attention retrieves by association, the maximum-likelihood objective has no term for truth, and left-to-right decoding commits to early tokens. Data, on this account, makes these failures worse rather than causing them. The account is usually argued rather than tested. We test it with interventions that need only sampling access. Study 1 holds pretraining data, tokenizer and scale fixed and swaps attention for a state-space mixer, using five Pythia/Mamba pairs from 130M to 2.8B parameters and four further attention models, on 111 facts presented with a planted false or a planted true statement. Swapping the mixer leaves free-recall failure unchanged (both 2.8B models answer 3 of 200 SimpleQA questions), but it changes what happens to a defect in the input. From 410M upwards, every attention model repeats the planted falsehood more often than its matched state-space model (2.8B: 650 vs. 566 of 666 items, p = 2.5e-20), also on facts both models know, while the state-space models can still read planted facts they did not know. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models. The correct fact cuts the share of answers with a downstream error from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works as well (p = 0.38), and the models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. The structural account survives in a narrower form. The mixing component decides whether a defect in the context becomes an output error, commitment decides how an error spreads, and on long-tail questions the first error comes from missing knowledge, not from a suppressed truth.

articles.title_original: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2606.23700v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

articles.agent: AI担当エージェント
articles.title_original: Learning Dexterous Manipulation Using Contact Wrench Guidance From Human Demonstration
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.00033v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dexterous robot manipulation can benefit from the abundance of human demonstrations, but transferring such demonstrations to robot policies remains challenging. We present Contact Wrench Guidance from Human Demonstration in Robotic Dexterous Manipulation (CHORD), a framework for long-horizon manipulation of rigid and articulated objects with reinforcement learning. The key idea is object-centric contact wrench space guidance: we represent human and robot motions by the forces and torques they can induce on the object, enabling similarity to be measured by the induced instantaneous motions. This guidance makes reinforcement learning more scalable for contact-rich dexterous manipulation. We further introduce a large-scale simulation benchmark with 4,739 bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, constructed from motion-capture datasets and reconstructed in-house videos. Evaluated on 1,831 benchmark tasks, CHORD achieves an average success rate of 82.12%, demonstrating strong scalability. CHORD also generalizes to whole-body manipulation from hand-only and third-person demonstrations, achieving a 90.77% success rate, and the learned policies transfer to the real world in both open-loop and closed-loop settings.

articles.title_original: Adaptive Reparametrized Time for Score-Based Diffusion Sampling
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.02137v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

articles.title_original: Listen to the Features: Voice Anonymization Driven by Content Embedding Matching over Signal Reconstruction
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.09767v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The paper presents a voice anonymization model focusing on preserving content rather than producing realistic speech. It relies on content embeddings extracted from a frozen pretrained wav2vec2 encoder. These embeddings are decoded into an anonymized signal using vector quantization and a HiFi-GAN vocoder, both trained on LibriTTS without any waveform reconstruction loss or speaker embedding mapping. The training objective enforces that embeddings of the anonymized signal match those of the original one. While training, an auxiliary speaker classification branch with a gradient reversal layer is used to discard speakerspecific information. Results show that this straightforward embedding-based approach achieves very low WER (2.53) with an anonymization performance (EER 13.39) ranking within first level for VPC. Notably, emotions are partially preserved (UAR 43.91), even without a supporting training objective, while the anonymized voice is audible without reconstruction loss.

articles.title_original: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2607.19181v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
  In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

articles.title_original: RamanPFN: A physics-guided spectral foundation framework for in-context learning across diverse Raman applications
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.02157v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Raman spectroscopy enables label-free molecular characterization across materials science, analytical chemistry, biomedicine, and industrial process monitoring. However, machine learning for high-dimensional spectroscopy remains constrained by limited labeled data and a mismatch between the physical organization of spectra and feature-agnostic models. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN predict in context without parameter updates, but on wide spectra feature subsampling preserves channel coverage while losing joint visibility: in the five widest tasks, every channel was covered, yet only 4.4% of random channel pairs co-occurred in any forward pass. We present RamanPFN, a general-purpose spectral foundation framework for unified in-context inference through physics-guided spectral learning, which encodes the additive mixing of constituent spectra and the locality of vibrational bands. Global Compositional Unmixing decomposes distributed, multi-band mixture signatures into shared non-negative bases to couple covarying peaks across the full spectrum, while Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding extracts orthogonal modes within contiguous spectral neighborhoods to preserve peak morphology, intensity fluctuations, and peak shifts. Posterior marginalization over admissible unmixings unifies both scales into in-context prediction without updating the model. Across 74 public Raman datasets exceeding 330,000 spectra, RamanPFN outperformed 26 methods spanning chemometrics, spectral neural networks, deep tabular learners, and tabular foundation models on 129 regression targets, reducing backbone RMSE by 13.2%. We demonstrate across TabPFN-3, TabICLv2, and Kumo-Tabular that this advantage generalizes to both regression and classification tasks, reducing regression error by 12.3%-25.7% and multiclass log loss by 42.4%-63.5% to enable data-efficient quantitative analysis and sample identification.

articles.title_original: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.09928v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.

articles.title_original: SplitLite: Low-Rank Residual Compression for Split Learning
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2608.23018v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of on-device large language models (LLMs) faces a significant computing burden. To overcome this limitation, split learning (SL) has emerged as a promising solution, which offloads the primary training workload to a powerful server. However, SL requires exchanging high-dimensional activations and gradients between clients and the server, resulting in prohibitive communication costs. To overcome this challenge, we propose SplitLite, a communication-efficient split federated LoRA fine-tuning method that exploits the low effective rank structure of consecutive-epoch activation and gradient residuals. Our key finding is that, under low-rank LoRA updates with the pretrained backbone frozen, the activation and gradient residuals of the same data sample between adjacent epochs exhibit low effective ranks, with most of their energy concentrated in a small number of singular directions. By exploiting this property, SplitLite transmits only quantized truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) residual factors, thereby significantly reducing both activation uplink and gradient downlink traffic. Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark across a series of advanced on-device LLMs demonstrate that our method reduces activation uplink communication costs by up to 93.5\% and total communication costs by up to 88.6\%, without sacrificing model performance.

articles.title_original: Reinforcement Learning over Patient Trajectories for Clinical Reasoning in EHR Foundation Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.12277v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models trained on longitudinal patient trajectories have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical prediction tasks. However, their clinical reasoning capabilities remain constrained by next-token prediction on limited and incomplete EHR data. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning framework that treats EHR foundation models as generative policies over patient trajectories. We formulate common clinical prediction problems (e.g., hospital readmission) as event-conditioned, time-windowed reasoning tasks. We then design time-aware, rollout-sensitive rewards to account for finite rollout lengths and temporally inconclusive outcomes. We find that RL fine-tuning consistently improves over pre-trained backbones and strong baselines. Notably, it enables smaller models to match larger pre-trained models in data-limited regimes and induces positive transfer across tasks. Further analysis shows that RL fine-tuned models generate trajectories with stronger structural and semantic alignment to ground truth and greater downstream utility.

articles.title_original: CIDERS: Cloud-Edge LLM Collaborative Learning via Accelerating Personalized Bilevel Optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.15664v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Amid the rapid advancement of physical-world intelligence, cloud-edge collaborative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising roadmap for practical LLM deployment. However, existing cloud-edge paradigms struggle to balance global consensus with local personalization, which fails to satisfy the need for a unified knowledge foundation on the cloud and domain-specific adaptation at the edge. To address this, we introduce, for the first time, a personalized bilevel optimization framework that formalizes cloud-edge LLM collaboration as a dual structure: the upper level optimizes edge-side personalization, while the lower level governs cloud-side knowledge transfer, reaching cloud-edge evolving in coordination. We then propose CIDERS, an efficient solver that decomposes the model into a learnable backbone and a messenger. While the cloud performs knowledge transfer to the learnable backbone, the key lies in embedding global trajectories into each local personalization step via consensus-variate correction to reconcile personalization with consensus. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis, including a geometric characterization of the local trajectory and a full convergence guarantee, revealing an explicit trade-off structure between personalization and global convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CIDERS consistently outperforms competitive baselines on the compressed edge path, with 3.1x and 1.7x gains on mathematical reasoning and code generation, respectively, and a 10\% relative gain on instruction metrics. Mechanism experiments attribute these gains to early consensus-corrected coordination and task-aware distillation. Overall, CIDERS offers a viable path toward consensus-guided continuous personalization in cloud-edge LLM systems.

articles.title_original: GraphToolbox: A Configurable Framework for Controlled Benchmarking of Graph Neural Network Forecasting
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.24609v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Electricity forecasting often involves spatially related signals observed over regions, substations, and feeders, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) represent these relations through a graph. Building a complete GNN forecasting experiment is nonetheless laborious, because graph construction, model selection, training, aggregation, and interpretation often require separate tools. We present GraphToolbox, an open-source Python framework that unifies these stages in one configuration-driven pipeline built on PyTorch Geometric. It offers data-driven graph construction, a single interface for most graph convolution operators of PyTorch Geometric and for recurrent graph cells, online expert aggregation, forecasting interpretability, and significance testing on forecasts. We use GraphToolbox to run a controlled benchmark: we compare architectural and modeling choices for French electricity load and net-load forecasting at regional and national levels under a common experimental protocol. On load, most evaluated graph convolutions outperform additive, recurrent, and foundation-model baselines. Pooled XGBoost, trained on the same inputs, has a lower RMSE than the best graph models, although the difference is not significant. Online expert aggregation and daily model updates improve accuracy further. On net-load, graph models outperform additive, recurrent, and XGBoost baselines, with further gains from forecasting the physical components separately. Statistical tests do not identify a single best convolution for load forecasting.

articles.title_original: Learning Perturbation Robust Policies for LLM Agents with Stable Optimization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.34064v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective post-training paradigm for long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents. However, we find that the resulting policies can be sensitive to various policy perturbations, such as hidden-state noise, pruning, and quantization. In this work, we study how to improve perturbation robustness during policy optimization. We first introduce the notion of a perturbation robust policy and analyze conditions under which perturbed policy updates preserve stable monotonic improvement. Based on this analysis, we introduce Stable Perturbation-Robust Policy Optimization (SPrPO), which applies adaptive and sensitivity-aware perturbations during RL training. We evaluate SPrPO on ALFWorld and WebShop and conduct systematic experiments across multiple perturbation types and scales, showing improved perturbation robustness while maintaining stable policy optimization.

articles.title_original: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2609.38166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of rounding errors and the presence of outlier rows and columns in the state. To address these challenges, we propose LeapQuant, a training-free method that achieves near-lossless performance under 8-bit recurrent-state quantization. First, to mitigate error accumulation, we propose per-window quantization, which leaps over a window of tokens and quantizes the state only once at its end. Within a window, outputs are computed from the fixed low-bit state together with high-precision buffered updates. Second, to reduce the error introduced by each quantization, LeapQuant retains the state's largest outliers as a few high-precision Compensator Tokens, which share the update path of real tokens. We then smooth the remaining residual before quantization to further reduce the error. Comprehensive experiments across the Qwen, Kimi, and GLM model families show that LeapQuant substantially reduces memory and compute costs during inference. With accuracy comparable to the FP32 baseline, it achieves average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs.

articles.title_original: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in LLMs with Whiteout
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.02418v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets, including content scraped from nearly every accessible website and user inputs. As a result, LLMs often memorize and reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. This leads to significant privacy risks, particularly for high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges. Existing mitigations largely rely on machine unlearning. However, these methods often remove more information than needed, degrade model utility and safety, and are highly vulnerable to attacks.
  This paper presents Whiteout, a practical tool that, upon requests by individuals, prevents LLMs from regurgitating their genuine PSIs, by overwriting them using precise and carefully designed obfuscation samples. We evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model. Results show that Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of the targeted PSIs, has negligible impact on model utility and safety, and outperforms existing alternatives. We also test Whiteout against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks like relearning and quantization. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on the security and ethical implications of Whiteout.

articles.title_original: CACHEFORGE: LLM-Guided End-to-End Generative Cache Replacement Policy for Performance and Hardware Efficiency
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.07668v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern cache replacement designs saturate because they operate within fixed representational structures, hand-crafted and heuristic based feature-engineered predictors, or offline imitation models that cannot generate new decision logic on their own. At the same time, replacement is shaped by the causal interaction of prefetching, thrashing, spatial locality, and access-type behavior, producing an enormous design space that is difficult to traverse manually. Prior approaches typically rely on heuristics, parameter tuning, or imitation of an offline optimal policy, capturing correlations rather than synthesizing new mechanisms. As a result, their performance gains often plateau and they overfit under dynamic workload conditions.
  CACHEFORGE is the first framework to evolve cache-replacement policies end-to-end by embedding a large language model inside a governed hardware-aware loop. In each iteration, the LLM proposes new C++ replacement logic, the policy is evaluated under a trace-based CRC-2 ChampSim simulator, and the framework enforces feasibility through reward shaping, structural checks, dynamic mutation, temperature scheduling, and cross-policy crossover. This closed-loop generation-evolution loop specifically designed for cache replacement policy enables the discovery of compact policies that satisfy hardware constraints while exploring algorithmic transformations beyond fixed predictor structures.
  Across SPEC CPU2006, CACHEFORGE outperforms all CRC-2 baselines. It improves the total hit rate by 27.36%, 19.69%, 13.72%, 13.15%, 11.83%, and 5.73% over MPPPB, ReD, Hawk-eye, SHiP++, LIME, and LRU, respectively. On memory-intensive workloads, it increases IPC by 10.15%, 7.89%, 6.34%, 3.64%, 3.12%, and 2.71% over LRU, MPPPB, LIME, ReD, SHiP++, and Hawkeye.

articles.title_original: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.16102v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tacit knowing, we argue, is an operating regime of one memory substrate, not a separate kind of content. In VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic hyperdimensional memory over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ realized as CASRAM and PyVaCoAl, one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With every collision repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks another; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path-integrated confidence $\mathrm{CR}_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes without being stated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is thus contingent or regime-bound, placing Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The same lemma answers a second dualism: the popular dual-process moral ("train slow, deliberate System 2 to tame fast, intuitive System 1") mirrors the two-store reading of tacit and explicit knowledge Polanyi rejected. Mercier and Sperber's reply, that reasoning is intuitive inference about reasons, matches Polanyi's; in the substrate, complete supervision is full rescue, which erases the valuation it should discipline. (4) Collins's three tacit knowledges map to bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (5) Our mentor-student DAG charts tacit transmission. (6) AI-solved problems with few follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted when LLMs generate, VaCoAl keeps the trace and the community values. (7) On Mercier and Sperber's theory, an LLM is a sophist: justification cut from tacit roots and evaluation. Truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, which we conjecture underlies evolvability and extends beyond humans. Testable predictions follow.

articles.title_original: Prune-and-Merge: Training-Free Scaling of Vision Transformers
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.18039v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.

articles.title_original: Hearsay or Fact? How Framing and Elicitation Shape LLM Probability Updates
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.27745v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We measure LLM probability updates on $\delta$-SNLI premise-hypothesis pairs across the Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) family. Separate calls elicit priors and posteriors; directional movement s signs changes by the annotated direction. We cross stated vs. reported wording with Direct single estimates (D0) vs. Multi-Candidate Weighted elicitation (MCW; five weighted estimates, V0, weighted mean M_W). Frozen formal tests cover 15 configurations (23,400 planned units): 3 primary (Qwen3-8B thinking off, OLMo-2-7B, gpt-6.1-sol via codex; 6,600), 4 CLI-harnessed configurations (gpt-oss-120b, claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-3.8-flash low/high; dnli-agy; 5,600), and 8 un-harnessed REST API configurations (dnli-api; 11,200). We add a 20-configuration, 8-provider dev ladder (3B-550B; 6,000 units) and a 2-model OpenAI 1+1+4 ablation of D0, Direct-CoT (D_CoT), MCW (V0), and Multi-Candidate Unweighted (MCU; V2 / M_U; 1,800 calls). All 15 reject H1 (s = +16.1 to +28.9 points) and H4a (endpoint reduction +0.065 to +0.391); 13 reject H2 (+2.0 to +8.9 points), except gpt-oss-120b (+0.9) and sf:qwen3.5-4b (-0.64). In 14 of 15 formal configurations, readouts obey Top-1 > MCW (M_W) > MCU (M_U). On 120 common pairs, API Qwen3 tracks local Qwen3 (H1 +18.72 vs. +18.90; H4a +0.265 vs. +0.254; H2 +3.78 vs. +1.67; H4b -9.03 vs. -6.70); local H2 rejects on all 240 pairs (+1.97), not this subset. API Gemma 31B (formal H4b -2.85, Top-1 +0.64; spread -13.3% / +7.6%) and Groq gpt-oss-120b (dev -4.15, +0.40; -18.4% / +12.2%) show small MCW costs and stated narrowing/reported widening without CLI harnesses. In OpenAI ablations, D_CoT keeps numeric-token entropy <1 bit; MCU (V2) shows smaller movement loss but halves spread and $\Delta H_2$ vs. MCW (V0). Because $\delta$-NLI annotates only direction, we make no claim about appropriate update magnitude. Code/data: https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies

articles.title_original: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.30468v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Scientific discovery requires more than generating hypotheses: ideas must be grounded in prior work, translated into executable methods, experimentally validated, challenged by counterevidence, and communicated through reproducible findings. Despite recent advances in autonomous research agents, closing this entire loop remains challenging in rapidly evolving computer-vision fields with complex training pipelines and expensive evaluations.
  We introduce SplatLab, an autonomous scientific discovery system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that integrates literature understanding, hypothesis generation, implementation, experimental refinement, falsification, and manuscript writing into a unified research pipeline. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, SplatLab identifies research opportunities, proposes novel methods, trains and ablates candidates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, and produces manuscripts grounded in verifiable experimental evidence.
  Unlike prior systems, SplatLab performs discovery over verified baseline implementations using domain-aligned modification scaffolds. A cascade-weighted Elo tournament evolves candidate methods using measured GPU performance and verbal-gradient feedback, while a standing falsifier incorporates adversarial stress testing directly into selection. An integrity audit binds reported claims to logged experiments, and reviewer-driven feedback can initiate further experimentation rather than merely revising text.
  SplatLab discovers methods achieving PSNR improvements of +0.18 to +3.78 dB over matched baselines, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, a previously unexplored setting for 3DGS. By closing the loop between scientific reasoning, executable experimentation, and evidence-backed communication, SplatLab compresses months of researcher effort into days of mostly autonomous compute.

articles.title_original: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2610.36202v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love trains", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, perform far worse. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.

articles.title_original: Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer for Joint Multipath Parameter Estimation: Applications to mmWave Positioning and Radio SLAM
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.01491v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Future 6G wireless networks are expected to evolve toward AI-native systems that support intelligent, environment-aware services, including positioning and mapping. Current research has already integrated AI into several aspects of communication, particularly wireless channel estimation. However, most learning-based channel estimators focus on communication-oriented objectives rather than explicitly estimating multipath parameters such as delay, angle of arrival (AoA), and angle of departure (AoD). These parameters provide essential geometric information for downstream tasks including positioning and radio simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). In this work, we propose a Spectral-Convolutional Factorized Transformer (SCFT) for joint multipath component (MPC) estimation from noisy complex channel estimates and physical beam-pair descriptors. SCFT combines local spectral convolution, permutation-equivariant beam-set attention, and a query-based Transformer decoder to detect and classify line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight paths and estimate their observed delays, AoAs, and AoDs. Experiments on realistic ray-tracing data show that SCFT reduces the generalized optimal sub-pattern assignment error by 13.1% compared with ResNet, the strongest competing baseline. We further demonstrate this advantage in independent snapshot positioning and radio SLAM, where SCFT reduces position RMSE by 18.5% and 65.0%, respectively, relative to ResNet. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly recovering multipath geometry, as improvements in MPC estimation can translate into substantial gains in downstream tasks.

articles.title_original: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.05726v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

articles.title_original: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.06706v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

articles.title_original: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.07342v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.

articles.title_original: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.07935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.

articles.title_original: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

articles.title_original: CulturalCrosswords: A Multilingual Benchmark of Answer Constraints and Grid Completion
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.10044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When several answers fit a riddle, exact-match scoring can penalise a valid response. CulturalCrosswords tests how answer constraints affect large language models (LLMs) solving cultural riddles, whose solutions draw on knowledge specific to a community. We constructed 53 crosswords from crowdsourced riddles in 42 languages and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five versions of each clue set: plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid. On 962 clues with alternative answers, lengths improve agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, compared with 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also receive credit. Part of the gain therefore appears to come from selecting a required answer form. Crossword input increases the share of all crossings with compatible answers by 9.7 points; requiring a completed grid reveals large differences between models. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy the correct cells.

articles.title_original: Split and Bridge: Multimodal Generation via Diffusion Bridging
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.10441v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Visual data are often expressed through multiple complementary modalities (e.g., images and segmentation masks), each capturing different aspects of the same underlying structure. Most existing multimodal methods adopt a top-down paradigm, learning a shared latent variable through joint training from scratch, which limits scalability. We propose Split and Bridge (SnB), a bottom-up framework for multimodal generation that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time. Rather than learning a unified latent space, SnB generates coherent multimodal samples by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point and then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. This design enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models without joint training, making it scalable and easily adaptable. Across standard benchmarks (PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ) and more complex settings (PIE-Bench++, ROCO), SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence. We show that SnB naturally extends to downstream zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Our results demonstrate that bottom-up generation provides a practical framework that complements existing top-down multimodal approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB

articles.title_original: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.10529v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

articles.title_original: STABLE: A Continual Learning Optimizer with Adaptive Drift Control
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.10655v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, leading to the loss of past knowledge and unstable adaptation across task streams. Existing approaches typically address this issue through replay buffers, architectural changes, or additional regularization terms. We argue that forgetting is a consequence of unstable learning dynamics, which may benefit from an optimizer-level solution. The main challenge is that learning dynamics are time-dependent, as demonstrated by empirical phenomena such as the stability gap. First, we formally prove that, for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition. Based on this insight, we propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer with adaptive drift control. STABLE enforces a drift budget by increasing the dual variable when the budget is violated and decreasing it otherwise. This results in high stability without penalizing plasticity. Experiments on long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods. In the multimodal setting, STABLE further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/atlas-luiss/STABLE.

articles.title_original: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.11306v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and $\texttt{robots.txt}$ directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and $\texttt{robots.txt}$, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

articles.title_original: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.11551v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.

articles.title_original: Direct Trajectory Optimization for Inference-Time Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.11821v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Alignment of text-to-image diffusion models with reward functions is a key challenge in controllable generation. Existing approaches typically rely on optimizing model inputs or fine-tuning denoising networks, which requires computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising models. In this work, we propose Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free framework that performs alignment by directly optimizing the sampling trajectory of diffusion models. Specifically, DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as the optimization variables, eliminating the need for gradients through the denoising network. To mitigate the out-of-distribution problem, we introduce Reward-Optimized Score Guidance, which interpolates between the optimized scores and the pretrained model predictions to stabilize sampling, while providing a provable theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions. Empirically, DTO improves alignment performance across three diffusion models on two benchmarks, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods while maintaining high efficiency. These results suggest that trajectory-level optimization is a promising direction for efficient and effective diffusion model alignment.

articles.title_original: Maze Runner: Autonomous Maze Navigation with Line-Based Localization and Control Barrier Functions
articles.body_original:
arXiv:2611.12949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.
